records.text: Owens cited the colloquial term Mormon Mafia as referring to the trusted Latter-day Saint businessmen and accountants Howard Hughes hired in 1960s Las Vegas.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: So the term Mormon Mafia, where does it come from? If you just Google it, you are going to learn that it is a colloquial term that is usually referring to, and I'll quote, the trusted latter-day saints inner circle of businessmen and accountants who were hired by billionaire Howard Hughes in Las Vegas during the 1960s. Okay, so Howard Hughes is the name that we need to reference.

verification.notes: TIME and the National Endowment for the Humanities both document the nickname Mormon Mafia for Hughes's small circle of trusted aides, predominantly Latter-day Saints, who handled business and personal needs during his Las Vegas years beginning in 1966.

sources.title: The Nation: The Keepers of the King
sources.relevance: Contemporary TIME profile of Hughes's so-called Mormon Mafia and their access and duties.

sources.title: Vegas's Revolutionary Recluse
sources.relevance: NEH history describes the Mormon Mafia nickname and the aides' business and personal responsibilities.

links.title: Mormon Mafia Term Traced to Hughes Circle

records.text: Owens said Howard Hughes shut RKO down for six months in 1948 to investigate every employee political leaning.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Now, he was so paranoid. This is a fact. fact that he shut down his film studio after he acquired it, RKO, for six months he shut it down to investigate the political leanings of every single employee.

verification.notes: Film-history references consistently report that after taking control of RKO in 1948, Hughes virtually halted production for six months while remaining employees' political views were investigated.

sources.title: Howard Hughes: RKO
sources.relevance: Summarizes the six-month shutdown and investigation of employees' political leanings with cited film-history references.

sources.title: Postwar Stars, Genres, and Production Trends
sources.relevance: Film-history reference documents Hughes's 1948 RKO takeover and political conflict with studio management.

records.text: Owens said Frank William Gay recruited the circle around Howard Hughes that became known as the Mormon Mafia.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: It was Frank William Gay who would then begin hiring people around him, hiring what became known as the Mormon Mafia.

verification.notes: TIME identifies Bill Gay as the Mormon executive associated with the six aides called the Mormon Mafia, while biographical accounts credit Frank William Gay with assembling the inner circle. The evidence supports the substance of the recruitment claim.

sources.title: The Nation: The Keepers of the King
sources.relevance: Contemporary profile connects Bill Gay to the recruited inner circle called the Mormon Mafia.

sources.title: Frank William Gay
sources.relevance: Biographical summary, citing HHMI and published biographies, credits Gay with putting together Hughes's inner circle.

records.text: Owens said the public was told Howard Hughes became reclusive because accumulated injuries led to painkiller use and severe obsessive-compulsive germophobia.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: He was in pain from injuries that he had endured over his lifetime. So he began taking painkillers and he then developed severe debilitating OCD, which made him avoid all contact with the outside world because he was a germophobe.

verification.notes: PBS and the American Psychological Association document the standard public account: severe injuries and chronic pain after Hughes's 1946 crash, long-term narcotic/codeine use, obsessive-compulsive symptoms centered on germs, and increasing seclusion.

sources.title: Howard Hughes (1905-1976) | American Experience
sources.relevance: Documents crash injuries, chronic pain, morphine addiction, germ obsession, and seclusion.

sources.title: Hughes's germ phobia revealed in psychological autopsy
sources.relevance: APA account of Hughes's germ phobia, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, codeine addiction, and reclusiveness.

records.text: TIME reported that Howard Hughes aides controlled which messages reached him, censored his reading, and controlled Hughes and his public image.
records.speaker: TIME

appearances.snippet: To reach him, they censored his reading matters. In short, they controlled Howard Hughes and the public image of him.

verification.notes: TIME's December 1976 profile says the aides decided which messages reached Hughes, censored his reading matter, and in practical terms controlled Hughes. The statement accurately summarizes that report.

sources.title: The Nation: The Keepers of the King
sources.relevance: Direct source for the claims about message control, censored reading, and control over Hughes.

records.text: Owens said Howard Hughes officially died of kidney failure on April 5, 1976.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Officially, Howard Hughes died of kidney failure on April 5th, 1976.

verification.notes: Contemporaneous reporting and later historical accounts agree that Howard Hughes died April 5, 1976; his official cause of death was chronic kidney failure.

sources.title: Hughes Autopsy Report
sources.relevance: Reports the official cause as chronic kidney failure and gives the April 5, 1976 death date.

sources.title: Howard Hughes (1905-1976) | American Experience
sources.relevance: Independent historical account of Hughes's April 1976 death.

records.text: Owens said Howard Hughes died aboard a jet owned by Robert Graf, whose company became Duncan Aviation.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: He was aboard a jet, actually, a jet that was owned by a man named Robert Graff, G-R-A-F. ... He was the founder of Robert Graff, Inc., which became Duncan Aviation. His business partner was Donald Duncan.

verification.notes: Historical accounts place Hughes's death aboard Robert Graf's Learjet while en route to Houston. Duncan Aviation's own anniversary history says Graf was a partner in the Beechcraft distributorship Donald Duncan joined in 1956, establishing the business lineage summarized in the statement.

sources.title: Howard Hughes
sources.relevance: Records that Hughes died aboard an aircraft owned by Robert Graf.

sources.title: Duncan Aviation 50th Anniversary History
sources.relevance: Duncan Aviation history identifies Robert Graf as a partner in the distributorship at the company's roots.

records.text: Owens cited an investigation as finding that someone administered Howard Hughes an almost certainly fatal and needless dose of codeine while he was virtually comatose.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: It was discovered after this investigation that, quote, someone administered a deadly injection of the painkiller codeine to this virtually comatose man, obviously needlessly and almost certain.

verification.notes: A post-death investigation for Hughes's estate was reported as concluding that a needless codeine injection given while he was comatose was potentially or almost certainly fatal. The official cause remained kidney failure, so this verifies what the investigation reported rather than substituting codeine toxicity as the official cause.

sources.title: Hughes Autopsy Report
sources.relevance: Contemporaneous report of potentially lethal codeine in Hughes while preserving the official kidney-failure finding.

sources.title: Howard Hughes: Death
sources.relevance: Summarizes the estate investigation's quoted conclusion about the needless and almost certainly fatal injection.

records.text: Owens said the investigation found five broken hypodermic needles in Howard Hughes arms and reported severe malnutrition, bedsores, kidney damage, and otherwise visibly healthy internal organs including his brain.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: certainly fatal dose we then learned that he suffered from malnutrition and he was covered in bed sores while his kidneys were damaged his other internal organs including his brain which had no visible damage or illnesses were deemed perfectly healthy x-rays revealed five broken off hypodermic needles needles that were inside the flesh of his arms when he died in 1976 his body was so thin that observers likened him to a captive from a japanese prisoner of war camp.

verification.notes: Published autopsy summaries report severe malnutrition and bedsores, damaged kidneys with otherwise healthy organs including no visible brain disease, and five broken hypodermic needles embedded in his arms. The details are consistent across the medical retrospective and historical reporting.

sources.title: Pseudo-Addiction: The Illustrative Case of Howard Hughes
sources.relevance: Medical retrospective based on Hughes's autopsy and government records describes his renal disease, pressure sores, and otherwise normal brain findings.

sources.title: Howard Hughes: Death
sources.relevance: Consolidates the malnutrition, bedsores, healthy-organ, and five broken-needle findings with published references.

records.text: Owens said the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints filed a purported handwritten Howard Hughes will that courts rejected during the estate litigation.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: And after he died on Robert Graff's plane, the fight for his $2.5 billion estate began. People just coming in saying, oh, no, I should inherit it. There was a mysterious handwritten note which was filed by the Church of Latter-day Saints, which they claimed was his last will and testament. ... That claim was summarily rejected by the courts. It was a 34-year legal battle. Until eventually it was decided that the majority of his fortune, around $1.5 billion, would be controlled by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the charity that I told you he started and that he had transferred the Hughes aircraft into.

verification.notes: A federal appellate opinion records that the LDS Church delivered the handwritten purported will for probate in April 1976 and that a Nevada jury rejected it on June 8, 1978.

sources.title: Dummar v. Lummis, U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
sources.relevance: Official court opinion documents the LDS Church filing and the jury's rejection of the holographic will.

records.text: Owens said Frank William Gay became a Howard Hughes Medical Institute trustee after Hughes died and was later discovered to have worked with the CIA at one point.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Of course, when he died, the trustee of the board became Frank William Gay, his trusted Mormon, who, it would be discovered later, was at one point working with the CIA.

verification.notes: HHMI confirms that Frank William Gay was one of eight original court-appointed trustees and served from 1984 to 2006. Public records document Hughes-company dealings with the CIA, but the reviewed authoritative sources do not establish that Gay himself worked for the CIA; that portion remains uncorroborated.

sources.title: HHMI Bulletin: In Memoriam Frank William Gay
sources.relevance: Official HHMI record of Gay's original-trustee status and service dates.

sources.title: Ford Library documents concerning Howard Hughes and the CIA
sources.relevance: Documents the broader Hughes-CIA relationship but does not establish Gay as a CIA employee.

records.text: Owens compared Kirk's final period to Howard Hughes relying on lieutenants, belatedly asking questions, and leaving an organization that reversed his beliefs.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: All of this just feels a little bit reminiscent to me, right? A man living his life one way, relying on his lieutenant, not knowing what was really going on around him. And then suddenly he picks up his head and starts asking questions. And now we see the organization that he left behind, the one that he built doing a complete 180 on virtually everything he believed.
